newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour to tackle tax and benefit reform.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour to tackle tax and benefit reform.

text.p: A Labour government would start reform of the tax and benefit system to reduce penal marginal tax rates on Britain's low-paid, Gordon Brown, the main opposition party's economics spokesman, said on Monday.
Brown told the party's annual conference that it was a scandal that tens of thouands of Britian's poorest families face effective marginal tax rates of as much as 150 percent.
"To help people move into work and to attack poverty in work, it is time to start tax and benefit reform as part of an integrated approach to modernising the welfare state," Brown said.
Labour released figures showing that the number of families facing marginal net tax rates of 70 percent had risen to 615,000 in 1995-96 from 290,000 in 1985.

"This is a system designed to keep the unemployed poor and the poor unemployed. That is a gross injustice and under Labour the tax and benefit system and the benefit tapers must be addressed," Brown said.
He reaffirmed Labour's long-term goal of a starting tax rate of 10-15 percent and contrasted it to the ruling Conservatives' ambition to scrap inheritance and capital gains tax.
"So, while the Tories want a millionaires' tax cut for themselves, I want a people's tax cut for jobs... one that will help thousands back to work," Brown said.

In a speech that was more about politics than economics, Brown argued that Labour's goal of a truly classless Britain would not only offer a fairer society but also deliver a more efficient and prosperous economy.

"We will only succeed when what each of us can achieve depends less on where we come from, what school we went to and what privileges we inherit, and more on our potential and on the opportunities we have to make the most of our potential."
Brown attacked what he called the crude free-market ideology of the Conservatives, based on the narrow pursuit of self- interest by the few at the expense of the many.

"A dogma that exalts the speculator, the asset-stripper and the instant millionaire of the privatised monopolies, the dogma that worships greed and privilege and condones short-termism at the expense of investment, hard work and opportunity for all," he said.
With one million men and women in Britain working for less than 2.50 stg an hour, Brown said it was time for Britain to join the civilised industrial world and implement a national minimum wage.

But he did not hint at a figure and likewise drew a veil over Labour's tax plans. Nor did the speech touch on Europe except for an oblique reference that under Labour there would be "no retreat into one nation isolationism".
